problem: VLN agents trained on R2R act in a graph-based simulator: they choose among neighboring panoramic viewpoints about 2.1 m apart and are teleported there. Before this paper, no one had shown whether such agents work on a physical robot in an unseen building, given real camera quality, continuous low-level control, and localization and navigation errors.
motivation: Evaluating only in simulation or only component-wise ignores real sensing, actuation and localization errors and system-integration problems, so it can give a misleading impression of VLN progress. The key observation is that the simulator's high visual fidelity comes at the cost of low control fidelity. The discrete nav-graph action space is the main thing that must be bridged to reach continuous robot control.
key_idea: Wrap an off-the-shelf R2R-trained VLN agent (EnvDrop) in a ROS harness. A learned subgoal model predicts nearby waypoints from a 360° RGB panorama plus a laser scan, emulating the simulator's nav-graph action space. ROS SLAM and move_base execute the chosen waypoint. Color-jitter domain randomization handles camera differences. Sim and real gaps are measured in a digitized twin (Coda) of a real office.
insight:
The sim-to-real gap splits into three measurable parts:
- **Camera/visual domain:** switching Matterport to Theta V images in sim costs -6.4 SR (Table 2, row 5 vs 4). Color-jitter retraining cuts this to -3.9 (row 6 vs 4).
- **Viewpoint differences on the real robot:** with a pre-built map and the GT nav graph, a further -5.2 SR (row 7 vs 6), with zero collisions or edge-traversal failures. This confirms the graph-simulator assumption that classical navigation stacks can reliably execute nav-graph edges.
- **Action-space abstraction:** replacing the nav graph with predicted subgoals and doing SLAM from scratch costs another -24.3 SR (row 8, SR 22.5). Only 29% of predicted waypoints fall within 0.5 m of a true neighbor (60% within 1 m). Both false positives (spiral staircase) and false negatives (narrow 80-90 cm gaps between bookshelves) occur.

So the language grounding learned in simulation largely transfers; the discrete-graph action space is the real bottleneck. This motivated continuous-action VLN (VLN-CE) and learned waypoint predictors.
method: Coda digital twin + dataset: 325 m² office scanned with a Matterport Pro2 camera (65 viewpoints, 6 removed; nav graph built from the visibility graph with edges ≤5 m) and imported into the Matterport3D simulator. 37 shortest-path trajectories × 3 kept AMT instructions = 111 instructions (1,334 m), collected with the R2R protocol; human follower SR 93%.

VLN agent: R2R-EnvDrop (Tan et al. 2019), which consumes ResNet-152 panoramic features (12 headings × 3 elevations), retrained with color-jitter domain randomization (brightness/contrast/saturation 0.3, hue 0.01) to mimic the consumer Ricoh Theta V 360° camera.

Subgoal model: 4-stage U-Net over a radial (range × heading) occupancy map from the 270° laser scan, with ResNet-152 panoramic features fused at the 3rd downsampling stage. It outputs per-bin waypoint probabilities; a confidence threshold keeps up to 5 waypoints as the agent's action candidates.

Subgoal training: trained on Matterport3D viewpoints with simulated 270° laser scans ray-cast against the mesh. Loss is Sinkhorn divergence between predicted waypoints and neighboring nav-graph viewpoints (excluding stair edges); the authors report it works better than cross-entropy.

ROS execution stack on a TurtleBot2 (Kobuki base, Hokuyo laser at 0.24 m, Asus depth camera, Theta V at 1.35 m): gmapping SLAM, amcl localization, and move_base planning and obstacle avoidance using laser + depth. The VLN agent and subgoal model run remotely as PyTorch ROS nodes.
Verification harness: mock ROS nodes replay simulator images and the nav graph; the ported agent matches the original EnvDrop performance within 1%.

setting.backbone: R2R-EnvDrop LSTM encoder-decoder agent over frozen ImageNet ResNet-152 features (trained on R2R) + U-Net subgoal model (trained on Matterport3D nav graphs)
setting.training_data: R2R train split, EnvDrop recipe, with random color-jitter domain randomization; the subgoal model is trained on Matterport3D viewpoints/nav graphs with simulated 270° laser scans. Nothing is trained or validated on Coda.
setting.observation: 360° panoramic RGB (Ricoh Theta V on robot, Matterport in sim) + 2D 270° laser scan (subgoal model, SLAM) + depth camera (obstacle avoidance only)
setting.action_space: Selection among up to 5 predicted waypoints (no-map) or nav-graph neighbor viewpoints (with-map / sim); executed by ROS move_base continuous motion
setting.simulator: Matterport3D simulator (plus a new Coda environment)
setting.privileged: 'With map' setting: pre-built laser occupancy map + ground-truth simulator nav graph as waypoint candidates. 'No map' setting: none (SLAM from scratch each episode); a separate map-based amcl stack is used only for evaluation pose tracking.

numbers_note: The only real-world benchmark is the paper's own single-environment Coda dataset (111 instructions), evaluated in sim and on the robot. R2R numbers are for the underlying EnvDrop agent they trained and deploy. Table 3 also gives pairwise NDTW trajectory similarity between settings, e.g. robot no-map vs sim Matterport = 0.31/0.33. Subgoal accuracy is given only in text: 29% of waypoints within 0.5 m, 60% within 1 m, 74% within 1.5 m. The Sinkhorn vs cross-entropy comparison is claimed without numbers.
results: The EnvDrop agent reaches 55.9 SR on the Coda simulator, versus 49.9 on R2R val-unseen, so Coda is in-domain. On the physical robot with a pre-built map and the GT nav graph it reaches 46.8 SR (43.9 SPL) with zero collisions. That is a ~9.1-point drop from sim: ~3.9 from residual visual domain gap after color jitter (6.4 without) and 5.2 from viewpoint misalignment. In the cold-start no-map setting using the learned subgoal model, SR falls to 22.5 (21.9 SPL), mainly because of subgoal prediction errors. The authors therefore call no-map transfer an open problem.
limitations: Evaluated in a single 325 m² office with 111 instructions; furniture was reset before each evaluation and some people were present, so generality is limited.

The no-map setting performs poorly (22.5 SR) because the subgoal model misses narrow passages and hallucinates waypoints such as a staircase; the with-map setting needs a pre-built map and a manually annotated nav graph.
Requires a 360° camera and remote GPU inference. The agent itself still uses the discrete graph action space; the authors suggest training with low-level actions in continuous simulators instead.
